clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia with a distinctive early sign: abnormal vertical eye movements, including dysmetric or slowed vertical saccades and impaired vertical pursuit, which may precede overt ataxia.
Caused by an unstable intronic pentanucleotide repeat insertion — an ATTTC insertion embedded within a normally present ATTTT array — in the DAB1 gene on chromosome 1p32.
DAB1 encodes Disabled-1, a key intracellular adaptor of the Reelin signalling pathway that governs neuronal migration and positioning.
Onset is usually in adult life, with falls, gait ataxia and dysarthria.
The disorder was originally described in families from Spain.
Repeat instability and anticipation across generations are features, correlating with the size of the inserted ATTTC motif.
Beyond the early vertical gaze disturbance the syndrome is relatively pure cerebellar, making the eye-movement abnormality the key clinical clue.
reference.pathophysiology: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 37 is an autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia caused by an unstable pentanucleotide repeat insertion within a regulatory intron of DAB1 at chromosome 1p32 — specifically an ATTTC insertion embedded within a polymorphic ATTTT array that is non-pathogenic when the ATTTC motif is absent. DAB1 encodes Disabled-1, an essential intracellular adaptor of the Reelin signalling pathway that directs neuronal migration and positioning; the inserted repeat is thought to alter DAB1 expression and splicing and to confer toxicity, leading to preferential cerebellar degeneration, notably of Purkinje cells. The disorder characteristically produces early abnormal vertical eye movements followed by a largely pure progressive cerebellar ataxia, and it shows repeat instability with anticipation across generations, placing it among the non-B DNA insertion repeat ataxias.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 and other relatively pure autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias
SCA5, SCA11 and SCA26 — further pure dominant cerebellar ataxias
Progressive supranuclear palsy, which causes a vertical gaze abnormality that can mimic the early eye-movement sign
Niemann-Pick disease type C, characterised by vertical supranuclear gaze palsy
SCA31 and SCA4 at chromosome 16q, other repeat-related ataxias
Other ATTTC-insertion repeat disorders such as familial adult myoclonic epilepsy and SCA10
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing for the DAB1 ATTTC insertion using a specialised repeat assay
Video-oculography or eye-movement recording to document the vertical saccade and pursuit abnormality
MRI brain demonstrating cerebellar and vermian atrophy
Hereditary ataxia gene panel to exclude other dominant subtypes
Investigations to exclude Niemann-Pick disease type C and progressive supranuclear palsy where clinically relevant
Family pedigree analysis with genetic counselling addressing anticipation
redFlags: Prominent vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with early falls raising progressive supranuclear palsy.
Cognitive or behavioural decline suggesting an alternative neurodegenerative diagnosis.
Organomegaly or young-onset systemic features pointing towards Niemann-Pick disease type C.
Rapid progression atypical for this slowly evolving hereditary ataxia.
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years to decades, with disability arising from a largely pure cerebellar syndrome; lifespan is usually preserved.
pitfalls: Dismissing subtle early vertical eye-movement abnormalities that are the key diagnostic clue.
Missing the diagnosis because standard panels do not detect the ATTTC insertion within the ATTTT array.
Confusing the phenotype with progressive supranuclear palsy or Niemann-Pick disease type C.
Neglecting to counsel families about repeat instability and anticipation.
